evidence: Prop. 1.2.29: ūnica nec dēsit jūcundīs grātia verbīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In this sense, charm or loveliness, Lewis & Short finds it only in poetry and in prose after Augustus, most often in Quintilian; in Cicero grātia is favour, influence or thanks. For charm of manner in classical prose, lepōs.

evidence: Lewis & Short: “pleasantness, delightfulness, loveliness”, of places

terms.comment: Lewis & Short: a poetic word, in prose perhaps not before the Augustan period, and frequent in Quintilian.

evidence: Plaut. Poen. 1.2.32: sine omnī lepōre et sine suāvitāte (Lewis & Short s.v. lepor)
Cic. Verr. 2.5.142: affluēns omnī lepōre ac venustāte (Lewis & Short)

sources: Lewis & Short: decor
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 289.
